title: Ἀντίνοος ξεῖνον βάλλει
about: Antinous, who has just refused the beggar, holds up a footstool as if to throw it, while the other suitors fill the beggar’s wallet. Odysseus begs again, flatters Antinous as the best of the Achaeans, and tells a false tale of his past: once rich, he was ruined by Zeus, went raiding in Egypt, and was sold to a stranger in Cyprus. Antinous orders him away from his table, and Odysseus answers that a man so stingy with other men’s goods would not give even salt from his own house. Antinous, scowling, throws the footstool and hits his right shoulder; Odysseus stands like a rock, says nothing, and curses him before the suitors. Antinous threatens to have him dragged out, and the suitors themselves rebuke him, saying that gods go about in disguise. Telemachus grieves in silence. In her chamber Penelope hears of the blow and wishes Apollo might strike Antinous; her housekeeper Eurynome wishes the suitors dead by morning. Penelope calls for the swineherd, and her speech to him goes on into the next part.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, καὶ θρῆνυν ἑλὼν ὑπέφηνε τραπέζης
κείμενον, ᾧ ῥ’ ἔπεχεν λιπαροὺς πόδας εἰλαπινάζων·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and a footstool taking he showed from beneath the table,
lying there, on which he was resting his sleek feet, feasting;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and took the footstool on which he rested his sleek feet as he feasted, and brought it into view from beneath the table, where it lay;
sentences.n: These words close Antinous’s speech, which ran from 406 to 408 in the part before; he now acts on it. ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη is ‘so he spoke’, ἔφη being the old past of φημί (the middle ἔφατο and φάτο are its relatives). θρῆνυν is the accusative of θρῆνυς ‘footstool’, and ἑλών is the aorist participle of αἱρέω, ‘taking’. ὑπέφηνε is ‘showed from beneath’ (ὑπό + φαίνω), and τραπέζης is the genitive ‘from under the table’. κείμενον ‘lying’ agrees with θρῆνυν. In ᾧ ῥ’ ἔπεχεν the relative ᾧ is a dative, ‘on which’, ῥ’ is ἄρα elided, and ἔπεχεν is the imperfect of ἐπέχω ‘rest on, hold on’. λιπαρούς ‘sleek’ is said of skin shining with oil, and εἰλαπινάζων ‘feasting’ is a participle from εἰλαπίνη ‘banquet’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἄλλοι πάντες δίδοσαν, πλῆσαν δ’ ἄρα πήρην
σίτου καὶ κρειῶν·
sentences.l:
But the others all gave, and filled then the wallet
of food and of meats;
sentences.i: But all the others gave, and filled his wallet with food and meat;
sentences.n: The suitors do what Antinous will not. δίδοσαν is an imperfect, ‘they were giving’, without the augment (Attic ἐδίδοσαν), and πλῆσαν is the unaugmented aorist of πίμπλημι ‘fill’ (Attic ἔπλησαν). πήρην is the accusative of πήρη ‘wallet’, the beggar’s bag. σίτου καὶ κρειῶν are genitives of what fills it: σῖτος is ‘food’, and κρειῶν is the genitive plural of κρέας ‘meat’ (Attic κρεῶν). The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 412.

sentences.t:
τάχα δὴ καὶ ἔμελλεν Ὀδυσσεὺς
αὖτις ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰὼν προικὸς γεύσεσθαι Ἀχαιῶν·
sentences.l:
and soon indeed Odysseus was about
again to the threshold going, as a free gift to taste of the Achaeans;
sentences.i: and soon Odysseus was about to go back to the threshold and taste, with no return, what the Achaeans gave;
sentences.n: The narrator says what Odysseus was about to do, and the next lines show that Antinous stops it. τάχα δὴ καὶ ἔμελλεν is ‘and soon indeed he was about to’: ἔμελλεν takes the future infinitive γεύσεσθαι ‘to taste’, and γεύομαι takes a genitive, here Ἀχαιῶν ‘of the Achaeans’. αὖτις ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰὼν is ‘going back to the threshold’, the threshold on which he sat down in the part before. προικός is a genitive of προίξ ‘gift’ used as an adverb, ‘as a free gift, with no return’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: στῆ δὲ παρ’ Ἀντίνοον, καί μιν πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπε·
sentences.l: and he stood beside Antinous, and him with a word addressed:
sentences.i: And he stood beside Antinous and spoke to him:
sentences.n: Odysseus, the subject, steps up to Antinous to make his plea. στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, intransitive ‘stood’ (Attic ἔστη), and παρ’ Ἀντίνοον is ‘beside Antinous’. καί μιν … ἔειπε is ‘and him … addressed’: μιν is ‘him’, and πρὸς … ἔειπε is tmesis for προσεῖπε, the preverb standing apart from its verb. ἔειπε is the epic aorist of εἶπον.

sentences.t: δός, φίλος·
sentences.l: “Give, friend;
sentences.i: “Give, friend;
sentences.n: Odysseus begs, and the whole speech is a plea to Antinous. δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι ‘give’ and has no object stated. φίλος is a nominative standing as a vocative, ‘friend’, where Attic would have φίλε. The unit is only two words, because it ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
οὐ μέν μοι δοκέεις ὁ κάκιστος Ἀχαιῶν
ἔμμεναι, ἀλλ’ ὤριστος, ἐπεὶ βασιλῆϊ ἔοικας.
sentences.l:
Not indeed to me do you seem the worst of the Achaeans
to be, but the best, since you are like a king.
sentences.i: You do not seem to me the worst of the Achaeans, but the best, since you are like a king.
sentences.n: Flattery: Antinous is called the best of the Achaeans because he looks royal. δοκέεις is uncontracted for δοκεῖς ‘you seem’, and ἔμμεναι is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (Attic εἶναι). ὁ κάκιστος is ‘the worst’, the superlative of κακός, and ὤριστος is ὁ ἄριστος with the article fused to ἄριστος by crasis, ‘the best’. βασιλῆϊ is the dative of βασιλεύς, and ἔοικας, the perfect of ἔοικα ‘be like’, takes that dative. οὐ μέν is ‘not indeed’.

sentences.t:
τῷ σε χρὴ δόμεναι καὶ λώϊον ἠέ περ ἄλλοι
σίτου·
sentences.l:
Therefore you ought to give, even better than do the others,
of food;
sentences.i: So you ought to give me food, and better food than the others give;
sentences.n: He argues that Antinous owes more than the rest. τῷ is the old instrumental of the demonstrative used as a conjunction, ‘therefore’. χρή is ‘it is necessary’, with σε and the infinitive δόμεναι, the epic infinitive of δίδωμι (Attic δοῦναι). λώϊον ‘better’ is the neuter comparative of ἀγαθός, and σίτου is a genitive of the thing, ‘better of food’; ἠέ (= ἤ) with περ means ‘than’, and ἄλλοι is ‘the others’. The unit ends at the raised dot early in 418, after σίτου.

sentences.t: ἐγὼ δέ κέ σε κλείω κατ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν.
sentences.l: and I shall celebrate you over the boundless earth.
sentences.i: and I shall spread your fame over the boundless earth.
sentences.n: His promise in return for a gift: to make Antinous famous. κλείω is the epic form of κλέω ‘celebrate, make famous’, from the same root as κλέος ‘fame’; with κε it can be read as a future or as a subjunctive, and either way it is a promise. κατ’ ἀπείρονα γαῖαν is ‘over the boundless earth’: ἀπείρων is ‘boundless’ (ἀ- + πεῖραρ ‘limit’), and κατά with the accusative spreads the fame over it.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ ἐγώ ποτε οἶκον ἐν ἀνθρώποισιν ἔναιον
ὄλβιος ἀφνειὸν καὶ πολλάκι δόσκον ἀλήτῃ,
τοίῳ ὁποῖος ἔοι καὶ ὅτευ κεχρημένος ἔλθοι·
sentences.i: For I too once lived among men in a rich house, a prosperous man, and I often used to give to a vagrant, to any man, whatever he might be and whatever he might come in need of;
sentences.n: Odysseus now begins a tale of his own past: once he was rich, and gave to beggars as he now begs. ἔναιον is the imperfect of ναίω ‘dwell’. ὄλβιος ‘prosperous’ agrees with ἐγώ, and ἀφνειόν ‘rich’ with οἶκον. δόσκον is an iterative imperfect of δίδωμι with the suffix -σκ-, ‘I used to give’, with no augment. ἀλήτῃ is a dative, ‘to a vagrant’. In τοίῳ ὁποῖος ἔοι the optatives ἔοι ‘might be’ and ἔλθοι ‘might come’ give a general case, ‘to such a man as he might be’; ὅτευ is ὅτου, and κεχρημένος ‘in need’ takes that genitive, ‘in need of whatever’. The tale is a made-up one, told in the character of a beggar.

sentences.t:
ἦσαν δὲ δμῶες μάλα μυρίοι ἄλλα τε πολλὰ
οἷσίν τ’ εὖ ζώουσι καὶ ἀφνειοὶ καλέονται.
sentences.l:
And there were servants, very countless, and many other things
by which they live well and are called rich.
sentences.i: There were servants without number, and many other things by which people live well and are called rich.
sentences.n: A list of what he once had: servants and goods. δμῶες is ‘servants’ (the word for those held in the house), and μάλα μυρίοι is ‘very countless, beyond number’. ἄλλα τε πολλά ‘and many other things’ is a second subject of ἦσαν. οἷσίν τε is a relative dative ‘by which’, with the epic τε that marks a general statement. ζώουσι is uncontracted (Attic ζῶσι) and καλέονται is uncontracted (Attic καλοῦνται); the subject, ‘people’, is not stated. ἀφνειοί is ‘rich’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ Ζεὺς ἀλάπαξε Κρονίων—ἤθελε γάρ που—
ὅς μ’ ἅμα ληϊστῆρσι πολυπλάγκτοισιν ἀνῆκεν
Αἴγυπτόνδ’ ἰέναι, δολιχὴν ὁδόν, ὄφρ’ ἀπολοίμην.
sentences.l:
But Zeus, Cronus’ son, laid waste—for he wished it, I suppose—
who me, along with raiders, much-straying, sent
to go to Egypt, a long way, so that I might perish.
sentences.i: But Zeus, the son of Cronus, brought ruin — it was his wish, I suppose — he who sent me off with far-roaming raiders to go to Egypt, a long journey, so that I should perish.
sentences.n: The false tale turns: Zeus ruins the rich man. Κρονίων is a patronymic, ‘son of Cronus’. ἀλάπαξε is the aorist of ἀλαπάζω ‘sack, lay waste’, and it has no object of its own; the house and wealth just described are what he ruined, and μ’ ‘me’ appears only in the relative clause. The dashes mark ἤθελε γάρ που as an aside, ‘for he wished it, I suppose’. ληϊστῆρσι πολυπλάγκτοισιν is a dative after ἅμα, ‘with raiders’, and πολυπλάγκτοισιν ‘much-straying’ comes from πλάζω ‘drive astray’. ἀνῆκεν is the aorist of ἀνίημι ‘send off’, with the infinitive ἰέναι, and Αἴγυπτόνδ’ is ‘to Egypt’ with the suffix -δε. δολιχὴν ὁδόν is ‘a long way’, and ὄφρ’ ἀπολοίμην is purpose with the optative, ‘so that I might perish’.

sentences.t: στῆσα δ’ ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ποταμῷ νέας ἀμφιελίσσας.
sentences.l: and I halted in the river Egypt the ships, both-sides-curving.
sentences.i: and I halted my ships, curved on both sides, in the river Egypt.
sentences.n: From here to 441 Odysseus repeats, nearly word for word, the Egypt raid told at 14.257–272; this line is 14.258, and the English follows the earlier rendering. στῆσα is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, transitive ‘I halted’ (Attic ἔστησα), and νέας is νῆας. ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ ποταμῷ is ‘in the river Egypt’: the name here belongs to the river. ἀμφιελίσσας is ‘curved on both sides’, a sense that is disputed, ‘rowed on both sides’ being another guess.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγὼ κελόμην ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους
αὐτοῦ πὰρ νήεσσι μένειν καὶ νῆας ἔρυσθαι,
ὀπτῆρας δὲ κατὰ σκοπιὰς ὤτρυνα νέεσθαι.
sentences.l:
There truly I on my part ordered my trusty companions
right there by the ships to stay and the ships to guard,
and scouts to the lookouts I urged to go.
sentences.i: There I ordered my trusty companions to stay right where they were by the ships and guard them, and I urged scouts to go to the lookout points.
sentences.n: Odysseus gives the orders that his men will break. This is 14.259–261. ἔνθ’ ἦ τοι μὲν ἐγώ is ‘there I on my part’, and the μέν is answered by the δέ of the third line, which sets the scouts against the guard. κελόμην is the imperfect of κέλομαι ‘order, urge’, without the augment. ἐρίηρας ἑταίρους is ‘trusty companions’; the sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known, and ‘trusty’ is the traditional guess. αὐτοῦ is ‘right there’, and νήεσσι is a dative in -εσσι. ἔρυσθαι is the infinitive of ἐρύομαι ‘guard’. ὀπτῆρας ‘scouts’ are sent κατὰ σκοπιάς ‘to the lookouts’, and νέεσθαι is the infinitive of νέομαι ‘go’. The unit ends at the full stop.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὕβρει εἴξαντες, ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ,
αἶψα μάλ’ Αἰγυπτίων ἀνδρῶν περικαλλέας ἀγροὺς
πόρθεον, ἐκ δὲ γυναῖκας ἄγον καὶ νήπια τέκνα,
αὐτούς τ’ ἔκτεινον·
sentences.l:
But they, to insolence having yielded, following their own strength,
at once, very quickly, of Egyptian men the very fair fields
were ravaging, and out women they led and infant children,
and the men themselves they killed;
sentences.i: But they gave way to insolence and, following their own strength, at once began to ravage the very fair fields of the Egyptian men, carrying off women and little children and killing the men themselves;
sentences.n: This is 14.262–265, and the English is the earlier one. οἱ δ’ is ‘but they’, the companions. ὕβρει εἴξαντες is ‘having yielded to insolence’: ὕβρις is ‘insolence, violence’, and εἴκω takes the dative. ἐπισπόμενοι μένεϊ σφῷ is ‘following their own strength’, with σφῷ the possessive ‘their own’, not a pronoun. αἶψα μάλ’ is ‘very quickly’, and περικαλλέας ἀγρούς is ‘very fair fields’. πόρθεον is the uncontracted imperfect of πορθέω ‘ravage’. ἐκ … ἄγον is tmesis for ἐξῆγον ‘led out’, and νήπια τέκνα is ‘infant children’, νήπιος being ‘without speech’. αὐτούς τ’ ἔκτεινον is ‘and the men themselves they killed’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: τάχα δ’ ἐς πόλιν ἵκετ’ ἀϋτή.
sentences.l: and quickly to the city came the cry.
sentences.i: and soon the cry reached the city.
sentences.n: The second half of 434, which is the second half of 14.265. τάχα is ‘quickly, soon’, and ἐς πόλιν ‘to the city’. ἵκετ’ is ἵκετο, the past of ἱκνέομαι ‘come’, without augment. ἀϋτή is ‘a cry’, the noise of the raid carrying to the town.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ βοῆς ἀΐοντες ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν
ἦλθον·
sentences.l:
And they, the shout hearing, with dawn appearing
came;
sentences.i: And hearing the shout, they came as dawn appeared;
sentences.n: This is 14.266–267a. οἱ δέ is ‘and they’, the people of the town. βοῆς ἀΐοντες is ‘hearing the shout’, with ἀΐω taking a genitive of what is heard. ἅμ’ ἠοῖ φαινομένηφιν is ‘with dawn appearing’: ἅμα takes the dative ἠοῖ, and φαινομένηφιν is a participle with the old ending -φιν, standing where a dative φαινομένῃ would. ἦλθον is the aorist ‘they came’, and the unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
πλῆτο δὲ πᾶν πεδίον πεζῶν τε καὶ ἵππων
χαλκοῦ τε στεροπῆς·
sentences.l:
and was filled the whole plain with footmen and horses
and the flash of bronze;
sentences.i: and the whole plain was filled with foot soldiers and horses and the flash of bronze;
sentences.n: This is 14.267b–268a. πλῆτο is the aorist of πίμπλημι in the passive sense, ‘was filled’, without augment, and it takes the genitives πεζῶν ‘foot soldiers’ and ἵππων ‘horses’. πᾶν πεδίον is ‘the whole plain’. χαλκοῦ τε στεροπῆς is ‘and the flash of bronze’: στεροπή is ‘flash’, the word used for lightning, here the glint of weapons. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος
φύζαν ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισι κακὴν βάλεν, οὐδέ τις ἔτλη
στῆναι ἐναντίβιον·
sentences.i: and Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, cast a terrible panic into my companions, and not one brought himself to stand against them;
sentences.n: Zeus himself breaks the raiders; this is 14.268b–270a, with στῆναι in 439 where Book 14 has μεῖναι ‘await’. ἐν δὲ … βάλεν is tmesis for ἐνέβαλεν ‘cast into’, with βάλεν unaugmented. Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος is ‘Zeus who delights in the thunderbolt’, from τέρπω ‘delight’ and κεραυνός. φύζαν … κακήν is ‘an evil panic’, φύζα being the fear that sends men running. ἔτλη is the aorist of τλάω ‘endure, bring oneself to’, with the infinitive στῆναι ‘to stand’. ἐναντίβιον is ‘face to face, against them’, from ἐναντίος and βίη ‘force’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: περὶ γὰρ κακὰ πάντοθεν ἔστη.
sentences.l: for around evils from every side stood.
sentences.i: for evils stood round them on every side.
sentences.n: The second half of 439, which is the second half of 14.270. περὶ … ἔστη is tmesis for περιέστη ‘stood around’. κακά ‘evils’ is a neuter plural with a singular verb, and πάντοθεν is ‘from every side’, with the suffix -θεν ‘from’. The clause gives the reason (γάρ) for the panic.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἡμέων πολλοὺς μὲν ἀπέκτανον ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ,
τοὺς δ’ ἄναγον ζωούς, σφίσιν ἐργάζεσθαι ἀνάγκῃ.
sentences.l:
Then of us many they killed with sharp bronze,
and the others they led up alive, for themselves to work by compulsion.
sentences.i: Then they killed many of us with the sharp bronze, and the others they led away alive, to work for them under compulsion.
sentences.n: This is 14.271–272. ἔνθ’ is ‘then’. ἡμέων is ἡμῶν ‘of us’, a genitive after πολλούς ‘many’, the object of ἀπέκτανον ‘they killed’, a second aorist of κτείνω in -ον. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ is ‘with sharp bronze’, the metal standing for the weapon. τοὺς δ’ is ‘and the others’, and ἄναγον ‘they led up’, ζωούς ‘alive’. σφίσιν is ‘for themselves’, ἐργάζεσθαι ‘to work’, and ἀνάγκῃ ‘under compulsion’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ ἐς Κύπρον ξείνῳ δόσαν ἀντιάσαντι,
Δμήτορι Ἰασίδῃ, ὃς Κύπρου ἶφι ἄνασσεν·
sentences.l:
But me to Cyprus, to a stranger who met them, they gave,
to Dmetor, Iasus’ son, who over Cyprus ruled with force;
sentences.i: But they gave me away to Cyprus, to a stranger who met them, Dmetor, son of Iasus, who ruled powerfully over Cyprus;
sentences.n: The tale carries him on from Egypt to Cyprus. αὐτάρ is ‘but, and then’, and ἔμ’ is ἐμέ. δόσαν is the unaugmented aorist of δίδωμι ‘they gave’, the Egyptians being the subject, and ἐς Κύπρον is the destination, ‘to Cyprus’. ξείνῳ ἀντιάσαντι is ‘to a stranger who met them’: ἀντιάσαντι is the aorist participle of ἀντιάω ‘meet’, in the dative with ξείνῳ. Δμήτορι Ἰασίδῃ is ‘to Dmetor, son of Iasus’, with the patronymic ending -ίδης in the dative. ἶφι ἄνασσεν is ‘ruled with force’: ἶφι is the old instrumental of ἴς ‘force’, and ἄνασσεν, the imperfect of ἀνάσσω, takes the genitive Κύπρου ‘over Cyprus’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἔνθεν δὴ νῦν δεῦρο τόδ’ ἵκω πήματα πάσχων.
sentences.l: From there indeed now here to this place I come, suffering woes.”
sentences.i: From there I have now come to this place, suffering woes.”
sentences.n: This ends the tale and his plea: the beggar in the hall has come from Cyprus, still suffering. ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, with the suffix -θεν. ἵκω is the present of ἵκω ‘come, arrive’; l keeps the present ‘I come’, and the English perfect ‘have come’ in i gives its sense. δεῦρο τόδ’ is ‘here, to this place’, τόδ’ being τόδε. πήματα πάσχων is ‘suffering woes’, with πῆμα ‘woe’. The closing mark ends Odysseus’s speech, which began at 415.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Antinous, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Antinous answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: the speaker changes from Odysseus to Antinous. αὖτ’ is ‘in turn’, ἀπαμείβετο ‘answered’ (ἀπό- added to ἀμείβομαι), and φώνησεν ‘spoke’, the verb of φωνή ‘voice’, with τε joining the two verbs. τόν is ‘him’, the beggar. No paragraph begins here, because the speaker simply changes.

sentences.t: τίς δαίμων τόδε πῆμα προσήγαγε, δαιτὸς ἀνίην;
sentences.l: “What power brought on this woe, an irksomeness of the feast?
sentences.i: “What power has brought this woe, a tiresome thing at the feast?
sentences.n: Antinous speaks, and his first words insult the beggar by calling him a woe sent by some power. δαίμων is an unnamed divine power, not a named god. τόδε πῆμα is ‘this woe’, the beggar himself, and προσήγαγε is the aorist of προσάγω ‘bring on’. δαιτὸς ἀνίην is an accusative in apposition, ‘an irksomeness of the feast’: ἀνίη is ‘trouble, something tiresome’, with the genitive δαιτός ‘of the feast’. The question mark here is the Greek one, the semicolon.

sentences.t:
στῆθ’ οὕτως ἐς μέσσον, ἐμῆς ἀπάνευθε τραπέζης,
μὴ τάχα πικρὴν Αἴγυπτον καὶ Κύπρον ἵκηαι·
sentences.l:
Stand just so in the middle, away from my table,
lest soon bitter Egypt and Cyprus you come to;
sentences.i: Stand right there in the middle, away from my table, lest you soon come to a bitter Egypt and Cyprus;
sentences.n: Antinous orders him off, and throws the beggar’s own tale back at him. στῆθ’ is στῆθι, the aorist imperative of ἵστημι, ‘stand’. οὕτως is ‘just so, as you are’, and ἐς μέσσον ‘into the middle’ (μέσσον is μέσον). ἀπάνευθε takes the genitive ἐμῆς … τραπέζης ‘away from my table’. μὴ τάχα … ἵκηαι is ‘lest soon you come to’: μή with the aorist subjunctive ἵκηαι (2nd person in -ηαι) gives a warning, and πικρήν ‘bitter’ stands with Αἴγυπτον and serves for Κύπρον too. The threat is a beating that will make those places seem bitter to him. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ὥς τις θαρσαλέος καὶ ἀναιδής ἐσσι προΐκτης.
sentences.l: How bold and shameless a beggar you are.
sentences.i: What a bold and shameless beggar you are.
sentences.n: ὥς here is exclamatory, ‘how’, and Murray prints it with an accent as if it were the adverb ‘thus’. ἐσσι is the epic ‘you are’ (Attic εἶ). θαρσαλέος ‘bold’ is from θάρσος ‘boldness’, and ἀναιδής ‘shameless’ from ἀ- + αἰδώς ‘shame’. προΐκτης is ‘one who asks for gifts, a beggar’, as at 17.352; τις with it gives something like ‘quite a’.

sentences.t: ἑξείης πάντεσσι παρίστασαι·
sentences.l: In order, to all you stand beside;
sentences.i: You stand beside every one of them in order;
sentences.n: He accuses the beggar of pressing every man in turn. ἑξείης is ‘in order, in a row’, πάντεσσι is a dative in -εσσι, ‘to all’, and παρίστασαι is the present middle of παρίστημι, ‘you stand beside’. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 450.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ διδοῦσι
μαψιδίως, ἐπεὶ οὔ τις ἐπίσχεσις οὐδ’ ἐλεητὺς
ἀλλοτρίων χαρίσασθαι, ἐπεὶ πάρα πολλὰ ἑκάστῳ.
sentences.l:
and they give
heedlessly, since there is no restraint nor pity
in giving freely of what is another’s, since much is at hand for each man.”
sentences.i: and they give heedlessly, since there is no holding back and no pity in giving freely of what belongs to others, for each man has plenty at hand.”
sentences.n: His reason for the suitors’ giving is the opposite of generosity: the goods are not theirs. οἱ δέ is ‘and they’, the suitors, and μαψιδίως is ‘heedlessly’. ἐπίσχεσις is ‘a holding back’, from ἐπέχω, and ἐλεητύς ‘pity’, here the sparing hand that a man has for his own things. ἀλλοτρίων is ‘of what belongs to others’, a genitive with χαρίσασθαι ‘to give freely’. πάρα is πάρεστι ‘is at hand’, with the accent thrown back, and ἑκάστῳ is ‘for each’. The closing mark ends Antinous’s speech, which began at 446.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀναχωρήσας προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him then, drawing back, addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then Odysseus of many wiles, stepping back, spoke to him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula with a participle that tells what Odysseus does: he steps back, since Antinous has just ordered him away from the table (447). ἀναχωρήσας is the aorist participle of ἀναχωρέω ‘draw back, retire’. προσέφη is ‘addressed’, and πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ (‘of many wiles’) is built on μῆτις ‘cunning’. τόν is ‘him’.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, οὐκ ἄρα σοί γ’ ἐπὶ εἴδεϊ καὶ φρένες ἦσαν·
sentences.l: “Ah! not then in you, besides your looks, were there also wits;
sentences.i: “Ah, you had no wits, it seems, to go with your looks;
sentences.n: Odysseus replies, and answers Antinous’s insults with a judgment on his mind. ὢ πόποι is the cry ‘Ah!’. οὐκ ἄρα is ‘not, it seems’, ἄρα marking a discovery, and σοί γ’ is ‘in you, at least’. ἐπὶ εἴδεϊ is ‘in addition to your looks’, εἴδεϊ being the dative of εἶδος (Attic εἴδει), and φρένες are ‘wits’. καί here is ‘also’.

sentences.t: οὐ σύ γ’ ἂν ἐξ οἴκου σῷ ἐπιστάτῃ οὐδ’ ἅλα δοίης,
sentences.l: not you would out of your house to your dependant even salt give,
sentences.i: You would not give even salt out of your own house to a dependant of yours,
sentences.n: A rich man’s stinginess, and the point of the whole retort. οὐ … ἂν … δοίης is ‘you would not give’, ἄν with the aorist optative of δίδωμι. ἅλα is the accusative of ἅλς in its sense ‘salt’, the smallest gift there is. σῷ ἐπιστάτῃ is ‘to your ἐπιστάτης’: the word is from ἐφίστημι ‘stand at, stand by’, and ‘one who stands by, a dependant’ is a guess from that root, not a certain sense. σῷ is the possessive ‘your own’. ἐξ οἴκου is ‘out of the house’. The unit ends at a comma, and the relative clause that follows describes the man.

sentences.t:
ὃς νῦν ἀλλοτρίοισι παρήμενος οὔ τί μοι ἔτλης
σίτου ἀποπροελὼν δόμεναι·
sentences.l:
who now, sitting among others’ goods, in no way to me brought yourself
of food, having taken from it, to give;
sentences.i: you who, sitting now amid what belongs to others, could not bring yourself to take any of the food and give it to me;
sentences.n: The charge in full: he sits at another’s table and still will not give. ὅς is the relative ‘who’, referring to σύ in the line before. ἀλλοτρίοισι is a dative of what belongs to others, and παρήμενος is ‘sitting beside’ (παρημένος). οὔ τί μοι ἔτλης is ‘you did not at all bring yourself, to me’: ἔτλης is the aorist of τλάω, with the infinitive δόμεναι ‘to give’. ἀποπροελών is the aorist participle of ἀποπροαιρέω ‘take away from’, with the genitive σίτου ‘some of the food’. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 457.

sentences.t: τὰ δὲ πολλὰ πάρεστιν.
sentences.l: and the many things are at hand.”
sentences.i: yet there is plenty at hand.”
sentences.n: The last clause of the speech: the plenty is already there to share. τά is the article used as a pronoun, ‘the many things’ (πολλά), and πάρεστιν is ‘is at hand’. δέ here is ‘yet’. The closing mark ends Odysseus’s speech, which began at 454.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’, Ἀντίνοος δ’ ἐχολώσατο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
καί μιν ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Antinous was angered in heart the more,
and, looking at him with a scowl, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Antinous grew angrier still in his heart, and, looking at him with a scowl, he spoke winged words:
sentences.n: The narrator answers the speech with Antinous’s anger. ὣς ἔφατ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο). ἐχολώσατο is the aorist of χολόω ‘be angered’, from χόλος ‘anger’. κηρόθι is ‘in the heart’, from κῆρ with the suffix -θι ‘at, in’, and μᾶλλον ‘the more’. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking from under (the brows), with a scowl’, with ἰδών the aorist participle of ὁράω. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is ‘spoke winged words’, the formula for words that fly from speaker to hearer; προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δή σ’ οὐκέτι καλὰ διὲκ μεγάροιό γ’ ὀΐω
ἂψ ἀναχωρήσειν, ὅτε δὴ καὶ ὀνείδεα βάζεις.
sentences.l:
“Now indeed not any more finely out through the hall, I think,
will you go back, since indeed insults too you utter.”
sentences.i: “Now, I think, you will not get back out through the hall unscathed, since you go so far as to utter insults.”
sentences.n: Antinous threatens him in two lines. νῦν δή is ‘now indeed’, and ὀΐω ‘I think’ governs σε … ἀναχωρήσειν, ‘you will go back’, the future infinitive of ἀναχωρέω. οὐκέτι καλά is ‘no longer well’, καλά being a neuter plural used as an adverb, and διὲκ μεγάροιό γ’ is ‘out through the hall’ (διέκ is δι’ ἐκ, μεγάροιο a genitive in -οιο). ἂψ is ‘back’. ὅτε δὴ καί is ‘since indeed also’, the ὅτε giving the reason, and ὀνείδεα ‘insults’ is the plural of ὄνειδος; βάζεις is ‘you utter’. His speech is only these two lines, so it opens and closes in this unit.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφη, καὶ θρῆνυν ἑλὼν βάλε δεξιὸν ὦμον,
πρυμνότατον κατὰ νῶτον·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and a footstool taking, he struck the right shoulder,
at its very root, along the back;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and took the footstool and struck him on the right shoulder, at its very base, along the back;
sentences.n: He does what he said. The first half-line is the same as 409, and the English follows 409. βάλε is the unaugmented aorist of βάλλω, here ‘hit with a thrown thing’, and δεξιὸν ὦμον ‘the right shoulder’ is the part struck, an accusative of the part affected. πρυμνότατον is the superlative of πρυμνός ‘at the bottom, at the root’, ‘at its very base’, and κατὰ νῶτον is ‘along the back’. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 463.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐστάθη ἠΰτε πέτρη
ἔμπεδον, οὐδ’ ἄρα μιν σφῆλεν βέλος Ἀντινόοιο,
ἀλλ’ ἀκέων κίνησε κάρη, κακὰ βυσσοδομεύων.
sentences.l:
but he stood like a rock
firm, and not at all did the missile of Antinous make him stagger,
but in silence he shook his head, evils devising deep within.
sentences.i: but he stood firm as a rock, and the missile of Antinous did not make him stagger, but in silence he shook his head, devising evil deep within.
sentences.n: Odysseus holds still, and keeps his thoughts to himself. ὁ δ’ is ‘but he’, Odysseus. ἐστάθη is the aorist passive of ἵστημι, used as ‘stood (firm)’, ἠΰτε is ‘like’, and ἔμπεδον is ‘firmly’, an adverb. σφῆλεν is the aorist of σφάλλω ‘make stumble’, and μιν ‘him’; βέλος is ‘missile’, and Ἀντινόοιο a genitive in -οιο. ἀκέων is ‘in silence’, and κίνησε κάρη ‘shook his head’. βυσσοδομεύων ‘devising deep within’ is built on βυσσός ‘depth’, ‘plotting in the depths’. The last line is the same as 491, said of Telemachus.

sentences.t:
ἂψ δ’ ὅ γ’ ἐπ’ οὐδὸν ἰὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο, κὰδ δ’ ἄρα πήρην
θῆκεν ἐϋπλείην, μετὰ δὲ μνηστῆρσιν ἔειπε·
sentences.l:
Back, then, he, to the threshold going, sat down, and down the wallet
he set, well-filled, and among the suitors he spoke:
sentences.i: Then he went back to the threshold and sat down, and set down his well-filled wallet, and spoke among the suitors:
sentences.n: Odysseus returns to his seat on the threshold and addresses the whole company. ἂψ is ‘back’, ὅ γε ‘he’, and ἰών ‘going’. κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο is tmesis for κατέζετο ‘sat down’, and κὰδ … θῆκεν is tmesis for κατέθηκεν ‘set down’, κὰδ being κατά with its last letter assimilated to the δ. ἐϋπλείην is ‘well-filled’, agreeing with πήρην. μετὰ … ἔειπε is tmesis for μετέειπε ‘spoke among’.

sentences.t:
κέκλυτέ μευ, μνηστῆρες ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης,
ὄφρ’ εἴπω τά με θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσι κελεύει.
sentences.l:
“Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen,
that I may say what my heart in my breast bids.
sentences.i: “Hear me, suitors of the renowned queen, so that I may say what the heart in my breast bids me say.
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to all the suitors, not to Antinous alone. κέκλυτε is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and μευ is the genitive ‘me’ (Attic μου). μνηστῆρες ἀγακλειτῆς βασιλείης is ‘suitors of the renowned queen’, βασιλείη being the feminine of βασιλεύς, here Penelope. ὄφρ’ εἴπω is ‘so that I may say’, the aorist subjunctive, and τά με θυμὸς … κελεύει is ‘what my heart bids me’, with τά the relative ‘what’. Line 468 is the same as 17.370, and line 469 is 7.186 word for word; the English follows the earlier rendering in both.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰν οὔτ’ ἄχος ἐστὶ μετὰ φρεσὶν οὔτε τι πένθος,
ὁππότ’ ἀνὴρ περὶ οἷσι μαχειόμενος κτεάτεσσι
βλήεται, ἢ περὶ βουσὶν ἢ ἀργεννῇς ὀΐεσσιν·
sentences.i: Truly there is no anguish in the mind, and no grief, when a man is struck while fighting over his own possessions, over cattle or over white sheep;
sentences.n: He puts his case: a blow taken in defence of property is no shame. οὐ μάν is ‘truly not’, a strong denial. ἄχος ‘anguish’ and πένθος ‘grief’ are two words for pain of mind. ὁππότ’ is ὁππότε ‘whenever’, with the aorist subjunctive βλήεται, ‘is struck’ (epic for βλῆται), a general statement. περὶ οἷσι κτεάτεσσι is ‘over his own possessions’: οἷσι is the possessive ‘his own’, easily mistaken for a relative, and κτεάτεσσι is a dative in -εσσι. μαχειόμενος is an uncontracted participle ‘fighting’. ἀργεννῇς is ‘white’, a dative feminine plural with ὀΐεσσιν ‘sheep’ (ὄϊς), and βουσίν is the dative plural of βοῦς.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ Ἀντίνοος βάλε γαστέρος εἵνεκα λυγρῆς,
οὐλομένης, ἣ πολλὰ κάκ’ ἀνθρώποισι δίδωσιν.
sentences.l:
but me Antinous struck for the sake of my belly, grievous,
ruinous, which many evils to men gives.
sentences.i: but Antinous struck me for the sake of my grievous, ruinous belly, which gives men so many evils.
sentences.n: Odysseus names the cause of his blow: his hunger. ἔμ’ is ἐμέ, and βάλε ‘struck’ is unaugmented. γαστέρος εἵνεκα is ‘for the sake of the belly’, εἵνεκα being ἕνεκα placed after its genitive. λυγρῆς is ‘grievous’, and οὐλομένης ‘ruinous’ is a participle of ὄλλυμι, which is also used as a curse-word (as at 484). ἥ … δίδωσιν is ‘which gives’, with πολλὰ κάκ’ (κάκ’ = κακά) ‘many evils’ and ἀνθρώποισι ‘to men’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ που πτωχῶν γε θεοὶ καὶ Ἐρινύες εἰσίν,
Ἀντίνοον πρὸ γάμοιο τέλος θανάτοιο κιχείη.
sentences.l:
But if anywhere of beggars gods and Erinyes there are,
Antinous before marriage the end of death may reach.”
sentences.i: But if beggars have any gods and Erinyes, may the end that death brings overtake Antinous before his wedding.”
sentences.n: A curse, and the last words of the speech. εἴ που is ‘if anywhere, if at all’, and πτωχῶν is a genitive of the ones whom the gods and Erinyes protect, that is, beggars. Ἐρινύες are avenging spirits. κιχείη is the epic aorist optative of κιχάνω ‘reach, overtake’, and the optative expresses a wish. πρὸ γάμοιο is ‘before marriage’, a genitive in -οιο, and τέλος θανάτοιο is ‘the end of death’, the end that death brings.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτ’ Ἀντίνοος προσέφη, Εὐπείθεος υἱός·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Antinous, Eupeithes’ son:
sentences.i: Then Antinous, son of Eupeithes, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula with a name and a patronymic: Εὐπείθεος is the genitive of Εὐπείθης ‘Eupeithes’ (Attic Εὐπείθους), so ‘Eupeithes’ son’. τόν is ‘him’ (the beggar), and αὖτ’ ‘in turn’. προσέφη is ‘addressed’.

sentences.t:
ἔσθι’ ἕκηλος, ξεῖνε, καθήμενος, ἢ ἄπιθ’ ἄλλῃ,
μή σε νέοι διὰ δώματ’ ἐρύσσωσ’, οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις,
ἢ ποδὸς ἢ καὶ χειρός, ἀποδρύψωσι δὲ πάντα.
sentences.l:
“Eat at ease, stranger, sitting, or go away elsewhere,
lest the young men drag you through the house, for such things as you say,
by foot or even by hand, and flay you all over.”
sentences.i: “Sit and eat at your ease, stranger, or else go away somewhere else, lest the young men drag you through the house — by a foot or a hand — for the things you say, and flay you all over.”
sentences.n: Antinous answers with a threat. ἔσθι’ is ἔσθιε, ‘eat’, and ἕκηλος is ‘at ease’. ἄπιθ’ is ἄπιθι, the imperative of ἄπειμι ‘go away’, and ἄλλῃ ‘elsewhere’. μή σε … ἐρύσσωσ’ is ‘lest they drag you’, with the aorist subjunctive ἐρύσσωσι (ἐρύω ‘drag’), and νέοι ‘young men’ are the suitors themselves. οἷ’ ἀγορεύεις is ‘for the sort of things you say’. ποδὸς ἢ … χειρός are genitives of the part gripped, ‘by a foot or a hand’. ἀποδρύψωσι is from ἀποδρύπτω ‘tear off’, used of skin, and πάντα is ‘all over’, an adverbial accusative.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ὑπερφιάλως νεμέσησαν·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they all then beyond measure were indignant;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and all of them were indignant beyond measure;
sentences.n: The suitors themselves turn against Antinous. ὣς ἔφαθ’ is ‘so he spoke’ (ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο). οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, the suitors. νεμέσησαν is the aorist of νεμεσάω ‘feel righteous indignation’. ὑπερφιάλως is the adverb of ὑπερφίαλος ‘overweening’, here simply ‘beyond measure’; the suitors are overweening themselves, so the word is ironic.

sentences.t: ὧδε δέ τις εἴπεσκε νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων·
sentences.l: Thus would someone say, of the overweening young men:
sentences.i: and one of the overbearing young men would say something like this:
sentences.n: A speaker is introduced: one of the young men, with no name. ὧδε is ‘thus’, pointing ahead, and εἴπεσκε is an iterative past, ‘would say’, built with the suffix -σκ- on εἶπον. νέων ὑπερηνορεόντων is a genitive plural, ‘of the overbearing young men’; ὑπερηνορεόντων is uncontracted (Attic -οῦντων) and comes from ὑπέρ and ἠνορέη ‘manliness’.

sentences.t:
Ἀντίνο’, οὐ μὲν κάλ’ ἔβαλες δύστηνον ἀλήτην,
οὐλόμεν’, εἰ δή πού τις ἐπουράνιος θεός ἐστιν.
sentences.l:
“Antinous, not indeed finely did you strike a wretched vagrant,
ruinous one, if indeed some god of heaven is anywhere.
sentences.i: “Antinous, you did not do well to strike a wretched vagrant, you ruinous man, if some god of heaven is perhaps here.
sentences.n: One of the suitors speaks, and he blames Antinous on religious grounds. Ἀντίνο’ is the vocative, elided. οὐ μέν is ‘not indeed’, and κάλ’ is καλά used as an adverb, ‘well, finely’. δύστηνον ‘wretched’ and ἀλήτην ‘vagrant’ agree. οὐλόμεν’ is the vocative of οὐλόμενος ‘ruinous’, a curse-word. εἰ δή πού τις … ἐστιν is ‘if indeed some … is anywhere’, and ἐπουράνιος ‘of heaven’ is from ἐπί and οὐρανός. The next lines show that he means a god who may be going about among men, perhaps this beggar.

sentences.t:
καί τε θεοὶ ξείνοισιν ἐοικότες ἀλλοδαποῖσι,
παντοῖοι τελέθοντες, ἐπιστρωφῶσι πόληας,
ἀνθρώπων ὕβριν τε καὶ εὐνομίην ἐφορῶντες.
sentences.l:
And the gods too, like to strangers from other lands,
becoming of every kind, go to and fro through the cities,
watching men’s insolence and their good order.”
sentences.i: For the gods also, like strangers from foreign lands and taking on every kind of shape, go to and fro through the cities, watching over men’s insolence and their good order.”
sentences.n: The reason for his warning: gods may walk the earth in disguise. καί τε is ‘and indeed’, with the epic τε of a general statement. ἐοικότες, the perfect participle of ἔοικα, ‘like’, takes the dative ξείνοισιν ἀλλοδαποῖσι ‘strangers from other lands’. παντοῖοι τελέθοντες is ‘being of every kind’, τελέθω being a poetic ‘be, become’. ἐπιστρωφῶσι is a subjunctive, ‘go about, visit’, and πόληας is the accusative plural ‘cities’ (-ηας for -εις). ἐφορῶντες is ‘watching over’. ὕβριν is ‘insolence’, and εὐνομίην ‘good order’. The closing mark ends the speech, which began at 483.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν μνηστῆρες, ὁ δ’ οὐκ ἐμπάζετο μύθων.
sentences.l: So then spoke the suitors, but he heeded not their words.
sentences.i: So the suitors spoke, but Antinous paid no heed to their words.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρ’ ἔφαν is ‘so they spoke’, ἔφαν being a plural of the past of φημί. ὁ δ’ is Antinous, the man they have been speaking about. ἐμπάζετο is ‘he took heed’, and ἐμπάζομαι takes the genitive μύθων ‘of the words’; with οὐκ it is ‘he paid no heed’.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχος δ’ ἐν μὲν κραδίῃ μέγα πένθος ἄεξε
βλημένου, οὐδ’ ἄρα δάκρυ χαμαὶ βάλεν ἐκ βλεφάροιϊν,
ἀλλ’ ἀκέων κίνησε κάρη, κακὰ βυσσοδομεύων.
sentences.i: But Telemachus made great grief grow in his heart for the man who had been struck, and let no tear fall to the ground from his eyes, but in silence he shook his head, devising evil deep within.
sentences.n: Telemachus feels what Odysseus feels, and shows nothing. ἐν μὲν κραδίῃ is ‘in his heart’ (κραδίη is καρδία), and ἄεξε is the imperfect of ἀέξω ‘make grow’, without augment. βλημένου, the aorist participle (middle-passive) of βάλλω in the genitive, is ‘of the man struck’. οὐδ’ ἄρα δάκρυ … βάλεν is ‘and no tear did he cast’, βάλεν being unaugmented, and χαμαί ‘to the ground’. βλεφάροιϊν is a poetic ending of βλέφαρον ‘eyelid’, probably a dual, ‘from the two eyelids’. The last line is the same as 465.

sentences.t:
τοῦ δ’ ὡς οὖν ἤκουσε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια
βλημένου ἐν μεγάρῳ, μετ’ ἄρα δμῳῇσιν ἔειπεν·
sentences.l:
But when she heard of him, circumspect Penelope,
struck in the hall, among her maidservants she spoke:
sentences.i: When circumspect Penelope heard that he had been struck in the hall, she spoke among her maids:
sentences.n: Penelope is in her chamber (506) and hears of the blow second-hand. τοῦ … ἤκουσε is ‘she heard of him’: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard about, and βλημένου ‘struck’ agrees with τοῦ. ὡς οὖν is ‘when then’. ἐν μεγάρῳ is ‘in the hall’. μετ’ … ἔειπεν is tmesis for μετέειπεν ‘spoke among’, and δμῳῇσιν is a dative plural in -ῃσιν, ‘to the maidservants’ (Attic δμωαῖς).

sentences.t: αἴθ’ οὕτως αὐτόν σε βάλοι κλυτότοξος Ἀπόλλων.
sentences.l: “Would that so you yourself might famed-for-the-bow Apollo strike.”
sentences.i: “If only Apollo, famed for his bow, would strike you yourself in this way.”
sentences.n: Penelope’s wish, a curse on Antinous in Apollo’s name. αἴθ’ is αἴθε, ‘would that’, and βάλοι is an optative of wish, ‘may he strike’. οὕτως is ‘in this way’, as Antinous struck the stranger. αὐτόν σε is ‘you yourself’, with αὐτόν emphatic. κλυτότοξος is ‘famed for the bow’, from κλυτός ‘famous’ and τόξον ‘bow’; Apollo’s arrows bring sudden death.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτ’ Εὐρυνόμη ταμίη πρὸς μῦθον ἔειπεν·
sentences.l: Her then in turn Eurynome, the housekeeper, with a word addressed:
sentences.i: Then the housekeeper Eurynome spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A new speaker, the household’s housekeeper: Εὐρυνόμη is ‘Eurynome’, and ταμίη ‘housekeeper’. τήν is ‘her’, Penelope, and αὖτ’ ‘in turn’. πρὸς … ἔειπεν is tmesis, ‘addressed with a word’, as at 414.

sentences.t: εἰ γὰρ ἐπ’ ἀρῇσιν τέλος ἡμετέρῃσι γένοιτο·
sentences.l: “Would that upon our prayers fulfilment might come about;
sentences.i: “If only our prayers might be fulfilled;
sentences.n: Eurynome takes up the wish. εἰ γάρ is ‘would that’, with the optative γένοιτο ‘might come about’. τέλος is ‘fulfilment, accomplishment’, and ἐπ’ ἀρῇσιν ἡμετέρῃσι is ‘upon our prayers’: ἀρή is ‘prayer’ and also ‘curse’, and here a prayer for harm. ἡμετέρῃσι is a dative in -ῃσι (Attic ἡμετέραις). The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: οὐκ ἄν τις τούτων γε ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ ἵκοιτο.
sentences.l: not anyone of these would Dawn, fair-throned, reach.”
sentences.i: not one of these men would reach fair-throned Dawn.”
sentences.n: If the prayer were answered, the suitors would die before morning. οὐκ ἄν τις … ἵκοιτο is ‘no one would reach’, ἄν with the optative; τούτων is ‘of these’, the suitors, and γε ‘at any rate’. ἐΰθρονον Ἠῶ is ‘fair-throned Dawn’, from ἐύθρονος, ἐύ- ‘fair’ and θρόνος ‘seat’. ‘Reach Dawn’ means ‘live to see the morning’.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια·
sentences.l: Her then in turn addressed circumspect Penelope:
sentences.i: Then circumspect Penelope spoke to her in turn:
sentences.n: A reply-formula: Penelope answers Eurynome. τήν is ‘her’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπε ‘addressed’. περίφρων is Penelope’s standing epithet, ‘circumspect’, from φρήν ‘mind’ with περί ‘all round’.

sentences.t: μαῖ’, ἐχθροὶ μὲν πάντες, ἐπεὶ κακὰ μηχανόωνται·
sentences.l: “Good mother, enemies are all, since evils they devise;
sentences.i: “Good mother, they are all enemies, since they devise evils;
sentences.n: Penelope’s answer to Eurynome. μαῖα is a respectful address to an older woman, ‘good mother’; it is also used of a nurse. ἐχθροί ‘enemies’ stands with πάντες, and the μέν is answered by the δέ of the next line. ἐπεὶ κακὰ μηχανόωνται is ‘since they devise evils’, with μηχανόωνται uncontracted (Attic μηχανῶνται). The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: Ἀντίνοος δὲ μάλιστα μελαίνῃ κηρὶ ἔοικε.
sentences.l: but Antinous most of all to a black death-fate is like.
sentences.i: but Antinous is most like the black spirit of death.
sentences.n: She singles Antinous out. μάλιστα is ‘most of all’. μελαίνῃ κηρί is the dative of μέλαινα κήρ ‘black death-fate’: κήρ is a power of death, to be told from κῆρ ‘heart’ by its accent. ἔοικε is ‘is like’ and takes that dative.

sentences.t:
ξεῖνός τις δύστηνος ἀλητεύει κατὰ δῶμα
ἀνέρας αἰτίζων·
sentences.l:
A stranger, some wretched one, goes wandering through the house,
asking men;
sentences.i: A wretched stranger is wandering through the house, asking the men for gifts;
sentences.n: She tells what she knows of the stranger. ξεῖνός τις δύστηνος is ‘some wretched stranger’. ἀλητεύει is ‘goes wandering’, the verb that goes with ἀλήτης ‘vagrant’, and κατὰ δῶμα is ‘through the house’. ἀνέρας is the accusative plural of ἀνήρ with the epic stem ἀνερ- (Attic ἄνδρας), and αἰτίζων is ‘asking’, from αἰτίζω. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 502.

sentences.t: ἀχρημοσύνη γὰρ ἀνώγει·
sentences.l: for want of means urged him on;
sentences.i: for need urged him on;
sentences.n: The reason for his begging. ἀχρημοσύνη is ‘want of means, need’, from ἀ- and χρήματα ‘goods’. ἀνώγει is the past of ἄνωγα, ‘urged, bade’. γάρ gives the reason. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἐνέπλησάν τ’ ἔδοσάν τε,
οὗτος δὲ θρήνυι πρυμνὸν βάλε δεξιὸν ὦμον.
sentences.l:
There all the others both filled it and gave,
but this man with a footstool, at its base, struck the right shoulder.”
sentences.i: Then all the others filled it and gave, but this man struck him on the right shoulder, at its base, with a footstool.”
sentences.n: Penelope’s account matches what the reader saw at 411–412 and 462–463. ἔνθ’ is ‘then, there’, and ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες is ‘all the others’, set against οὗτος δέ ‘but this man’, Antinous. ἐνέπλησάν τ’ ἔδοσάν τε is ‘both filled and gave’: ἐνέπλησαν has no object in the Greek, and the wallet of 411 is the likely one. θρήνυι is a dative, ‘with a footstool’, and πρυμνόν is ‘at its base’ (compare πρυμνότατον at 463). βάλε δεξιὸν ὦμον is ‘struck the right shoulder’. The closing mark ends her speech, which began at 499.

sentences.t:
ἡ μὲν ἄρ’ ὣς ἀγόρευε μετὰ δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν,
ἡμένη ἐν θαλάμῳ·
sentences.l:
She, then, so spoke among the maidservant women,
sitting in her chamber;
sentences.i: So she spoke among her maids, sitting in her chamber;
sentences.n: Penelope’s speech is over, and the scene shifts between two places. ἡ μὲν … ὁ δ’ is ‘she on one side … he on the other’, ἡ being Penelope. ἀγόρευε is an imperfect without the augment (Attic ἠγόρευε), ‘was speaking’. μετὰ δμῳῇσι γυναιξίν is ‘among the maidservant women’, and ἡμένη is ‘sitting’. θαλάμῳ is ‘in the chamber’. The unit ends at the raised dot in the middle of 506.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἐδείπνεε δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: and he was dining, heavenly Odysseus;
sentences.i: while heavenly Odysseus was at his meal;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, set against ἡ μὲν of the line before. ἐδείπνεε is an uncontracted imperfect (Attic ἐδείπνει), ‘was dining’, from δεῖπνον ‘meal’. δῖος is Odysseus’s standing epithet, ‘heavenly’. The unit ends at the raised dot.

sentences.t: ἡ δ’ ἐπὶ οἷ καλέσασα προσηύδα δῖον ὑφορβόν·
sentences.l: and she, to herself calling, spoke to the heavenly swineherd:
sentences.i: and she called the heavenly swineherd to her side and spoke to him:
sentences.n: Penelope now sends for Eumaeus; her speech to him begins in the next part, so there is no opening mark here. ἡ δ’ is ‘and she’, and ἐπὶ οἷ καλέσασα is ‘calling to herself’: οἷ is the dative of the pronoun ‘to her’. προσηύδα is ‘spoke to’, and δῖον ὑφορβόν is ‘the heavenly swineherd’, ὑφορβός being from ὑπό and φέρβω ‘feed’. Both verbs take δῖον ὑφορβόν as their object.
